proofs.proof_tex:
Fix an experiment horizon \(n\geq 1\), a policy \(\pi_n\in\Pi_n\), and a mean vector \(\mu\in\mathbb R^K\).  For \(j\in\mathcal J\) and \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define the one-step factor
\[
D_{j,i}:=\exp\!\left\{\mathbf 1\{A_i=j\}\left(\frac{Y_i}{\sqrt n}-\frac{1}{2n}\right)\right\},
\]
and define \(E^{(n)}_{j,s}:=\prod_{i=1}^sD_{j,i}\), with \(E^{(n)}_{j,0}:=1\).  These are proof intermediates.  By the definitions of \(S_{j,n}\), \(N_{j,n}\), \(X_{j,n}\), and \(Q_{j,n}\),
\[
E^{(n)}_{j,n}
=\exp\!\left\{\frac{S_{j,n}}{\sqrt n}-\frac{N_{j,n}}{2n}\right\}
=\exp\{X_{j,n}-Q_{j,n}/2\}
=E_{j,n},
\]
where the last equality is the elementary e-value specified by Definition \(\mathrm{def:fixed\text{-}closed\text{-}e\text{-}test}\).

Let \(p_{i,j}:=\mathbb P_\mu^{\pi_n}(A_i=j\mid\mathcal F_{i-1})\).  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:finite\text{-}predictability}\) and Definition \(\mathrm{def:finite\text{-}policy\text{-}class}\) make \(p_{i,j}\) an \(\mathcal F_{i-1}\)-measurable random variable taking values in \([0,1]\).  Under Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:gaussian\text{-}known\text{-}variance}\), conditional on \(\mathcal F_{i-1}\) and \(A_i=j\), the density of \(Y_i\) is \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp\{-(y-\mu_j)^2/2\}\).  Completing the square gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E_\mu^{\pi_n}\!\left[
 \exp\!\left\{\frac{Y_i}{\sqrt n}-\frac{1}{2n}\right\}
 \mathrel{\Big|}\mathcal F_{i-1},A_i=j
\right]\\
&\quad=\int_{\mathbb R}
 \exp\!\left\{\frac{y}{\sqrt n}-\frac{1}{2n}\right\}
 \frac{\exp\{-(y-\mu_j)^2/2\}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,dy\\
&\quad=\exp\!\left\{\frac{\mu_j}{\sqrt n}\right\}
 \int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\exp\{-(y-\mu_j-n^{-1/2})^2/2\}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,dy
=\exp\!\left\{\frac{\mu_j}{\sqrt n}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(A_i\neq j\), then \(D_{j,i}=1\).  Consequently, conditioning first on \((\mathcal F_{i-1},A_i)\) and then on \(\mathcal F_{i-1}\),
\[
\mathbb E_\mu^{\pi_n}[D_{j,i}\mid\mathcal F_{i-1}]
=1+p_{i,j}\left(\exp\!\left\{\frac{\mu_j}{\sqrt n}\right\}-1\right).
\]
For every true elementary null, meaning every \(j\) with \(\mu_j\leq0\), the right-hand side is at most one.  Since \(E^{(n)}_{j,i-1}\) is nonnegative and \(\mathcal F_{i-1}\)-measurable, the preceding display yields
\[
\mathbb E_\mu^{\pi_n}[E^{(n)}_{j,i}\mid\mathcal F_{i-1}]
=E^{(n)}_{j,i-1}\mathbb E_\mu^{\pi_n}[D_{j,i}\mid\mathcal F_{i-1}]
\leq E^{(n)}_{j,i-1}.
\]
Thus \((E^{(n)}_{j,s})_{s=0}^n\) is a nonnegative supermartingale under \(\mu_j\leq0\).  Iterating the tower identity from its initial value one proves, rather than assumes,
\[
\mathbb E_\mu^{\pi_n}[E_{j,n}]
=\mathbb E_\mu^{\pi_n}[E^{(n)}_{j,n}]
\leq E^{(n)}_{j,0}=1.
\]
This argument permits \(p_{i,j}=0\), so no positivity or forced-exploration condition is being used.

Let \(T(\mu):=\{j\in\mathcal J:\mu_j\leq0\}\) be the set of true elementary nulls.  If \(T(\mu)=\varnothing\), then the familywise-error event is empty and its probability is zero.  Suppose henceforth that \(T(\mu)\neq\varnothing\).  Since \(T(\mu)\in\mathcal I\), Definition \(\mathrm{def:fixed\text{-}closed\text{-}e\text{-}test}\) gives the intersection e-value
\[
E_{T(\mu),n}=\frac{1}{|T(\mu)|}\sum_{j\in T(\mu)}E_{j,n}.
\]
Linearity of expectation and the preceding null-coordinate bounds imply
\[
\mathbb E_\mu^{\pi_n}[E_{T(\mu),n}]
=\frac{1}{|T(\mu)|}\sum_{j\in T(\mu)}
 \mathbb E_\mu^{\pi_n}[E_{j,n}]
\leq1.
\]
This is the arithmetic e-merging step specialized to the present construction and proved directly.

If some \(j\in T(\mu)\) belongs to \(\mathcal R_n\), then \(a_{j,n}\geq0\).  By the definition
\[
a_{j,n}=\min_{I\in\mathcal I:\,j\in I}(E_{I,n}-c_\alpha),
\]
every term in this finite minimum is nonnegative.  In particular, taking \(I=T(\mu)\), which contains \(j\), gives \(E_{T(\mu),n}\geq c_\alpha\).  Hence the deterministic closed-testing inclusion is
\[
\{\mathcal R_n\cap T(\mu)\neq\varnothing\}
\subseteq\{E_{T(\mu),n}\geq c_\alpha\}.
\]
Because \(E_{T(\mu),n}\geq0\),
\[
\mathbb E_\mu^{\pi_n}[E_{T(\mu),n}]
\geq
\mathbb E_\mu^{\pi_n}\!\left[E_{T(\mu),n}
 \mathbf 1\{E_{T(\mu),n}\geq c_\alpha\}\right]
\geq c_\alpha\,
\mathbb P_\mu^{\pi_n}\{E_{T(\mu),n}\geq c_\alpha\}.
\]
Combining the last three displays with \(c_\alpha=1/\alpha=20\) proves
\[
\mathbb P_\mu^{\pi_n}\!\left\{
 \mathcal R_n\cap\{j\in\mathcal J:\mu_j\leq0\}\neq\varnothing
\right\}
\leq \frac{1}{c_\alpha}=\alpha=0.05.
\]

For the smallest stress test, take \(K=2\) and \(n=1\).  Conditional on either possible assignment \(A_1\in\{1,2\}\), a null coordinate's factor is respectively \(\exp\{Y_1-1/2\}\) or \(1\); averaging over an arbitrary recruitment probability gives exactly \(1+p_{1,j}(e^{\mu_j}-1)\leq1\).  If there is one true null, its rejection requires its singleton e-value to reach \(20\); if both nulls are true, rejection of either requires \((E_{1,1}+E_{2,1})/2\geq20\); and if neither is true, the error event is empty.  Thus every assignment and the boundary choices \(p_{1,j}\in\{0,1\}\), including permanent non-recruitment of one subgroup, satisfy the same bound.

For a fixed scenario \(m\), write
\[
\ell_{m,\delta}^{\pm}(x,q)
:=\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}w_j\mathbf 1\{h_j^m>0\}
 f_\delta^\pm(a_j(x,q)).
\]
The scalar definitions give, for every \(a\in\mathbb R\),
\[
0\leq f_\delta^-(a)\leq\mathbf 1\{a<0\}
\leq f_\delta^+(a)\leq1.
\]
Because the weights are positive and sum to one, all three resulting losses take values in \([0,1]\).  In particular, Definition \(\mathrm{def:terminal\text{-}envelopes}\) immediately gives
\[
0\leq B_{n,\delta}^+(\lambda)-B_{n,\delta}^-(\lambda),
\qquad
0\leq B_\delta^+(\lambda)-B_\delta^-(\lambda).
\]

We next construct the comparison policy.  Fix an admissible finite policy \(\pi_n\) and a number \(e>0\).  The transformed policy \(\pi_n^{e}\) presents to \(\pi_n\), after each observation from subgroup \(j\), the virtual observation \(Y_i-e/\sqrt n\), while retaining the actual subgroup labels and the actual allocation clocks.  This rule is \(\mathcal F_{i-1}\)-predictable by Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:finite\text{-}predictability}\), and it is independent of the scenario label, so it belongs to \(\Pi_n\) by Definition \(\mathrm{def:finite\text{-}policy\text{-}class}\).  Under actual local drift \(h^m+e\mathbf 1\), Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass:gaussian\text{-}known\text{-}variance}\) and \(\mathrm{ass:local\text{-}scenario\text{-}scaling}\) show that each virtual observation from arm \(j\) has law
\[
\mathcal N\!\left(\frac{h_j^m+e}{\sqrt n}-\frac e{\sqrt n},1\right)
=\mathcal N\!\left(\frac{h_j^m}{\sqrt n},1\right).
\]
Induction over the observed filtration therefore proves that the virtual score-clock pair under \((h^m+e\mathbf 1,\pi_n^e)\) has exactly the law of the original pair under \((h^m,\pi_n)\).  At the terminal time the actual and virtual elementary e-values satisfy
\[
E_j^{\mathrm{act}}
=\exp\{X_j^{\mathrm{virt}}+eQ_j-Q_j/2\}
=E_j^{\mathrm{virt}}\exp(eQ_j).
\tag{1}
\]
The continuous construction is identical: the transformed control \(u^e\) feeds \(u\) the progressively measurable virtual score \(X-eQ\).  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:continuous\text{-}observed\text{-}control}\) and Definition \(\mathrm{def:continuous\text{-}control\text{-}class}\) imply \(u^e\in\mathcal U\), and
\[
d(X_j-eQ_j)=h_j^m u_j\,dt+\sqrt{u_j}\,dW_j
\]
under drift \(h^m+e\mathbf 1\).  Thus the same law identity and (1) hold.

For either experiment, compare the two observed laws generated by the same transformed policy at drifts \(h^m\) and \(h^m+e\mathbf 1\).  In finite time, the conditional Gaussian relative entropy contributed by observation \(i\) is
\[
\frac12\left(\frac e{\sqrt n}\right)^2=\frac{e^2}{2n}.
\]
The assignment kernels agree conditionally on the observed past and hence contribute zero.  The chain rule and the fixed horizon give total relative entropy \(e^2/2\).  In continuous time, the likelihood exponential has integrand \(e\sqrt{u_j(t)}\) on coordinate \(j\), and its energy is
\[
\frac12\int_0^1 e^2\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}u_j(t)\,dt
=\frac{e^2}{2},
\]
because \(u(t)\in\Delta(\mathcal J)\).  The same entropy identity follows first for simple predictable controls by conditional Gaussian integration and then for all progressively measurable controls by bounded-energy approximation.

For completeness, the needed total-variation inequality follows from this entropy identity without an additional probabilistic assumption.  If \(P\ll Q\), let \(A=\{dP/dQ\geq1\}\).  The log-sum inequality applied to \(A\) and \(A^c\) gives
\[
D(P\Vert Q)\geq
P(A)\log\frac{P(A)}{Q(A)}
+(1-P(A))\log\frac{1-P(A)}{1-Q(A)}.
\]
For fixed \(Q(A)\), the right side has second derivative
\(1/[p(1-p)]\geq4\), vanishes with its first derivative at
\(p=Q(A)\), and is therefore at least
\(2(P(A)-Q(A))^2\).  Since \(P(A)-Q(A)=\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\),
\[
\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\leq\sqrt{D(P\Vert Q)/2}\leq e/2.
\tag{2}
\]

We now control small clocks.  Under either admissible policy and scenario \(m\), the observations of subgroup \(j\), arranged in their own information time, have the score-stack representation
\[
X_j(q)=h_j^m q+W_j(q),\qquad 0\leq q\leq1,
\]
with a standard Brownian motion \(W_j\); in the finite experiment only the grid points of this stack are inspected.  This representation follows directly by concatenating the independent centered unit-Gaussian observations, and remains valid at predictable information times.  Define
\[
\mathcal E_{\eta,\delta}
:=\bigcup_{j\in\mathcal J}
\left\{\sup_{0\leq q\leq\eta}
\exp\{h_j^m q+W_j(q)-q/2\}\geq20-\delta\right\}.
\]
Since \(|h_j^m|\leq H\), occurrence of the event for coordinate \(j\) implies
\[
\sup_{0\leq q\leq\eta}W_j(q)
\geq \log(20-\delta)-H\eta.
\]
Reflecting Brownian paths after their first passage of a positive level and then using the elementary Gaussian Chernoff bound yields
\[
\Pr(\mathcal E_{\eta,\delta})
\leq
\min\left\{1,\,
2K\exp\!\left[
-\frac{(\log(20-\delta)-H\eta)_+^2}{2\eta}
\right]\right\}.
\tag{3}
\]
The finite-grid event is a subset of the continuous supremum event, so (3) applies uniformly in \(n\).

Set
\[
e=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{shift}}(\delta,\eta)
=\eta^{-1}\log\!\left(1+\frac{2K\delta}{20-\delta}\right).
\]
Outside \(\mathcal E_{\eta,\delta}\), if an intersection e-value satisfies
\(E_I>20-\delta\), at least one constituent \(k\in I\) satisfies
\(E_k>20-\delta\), and every such constituent has \(Q_k>\eta\).
Consequently (1), \(|I|\leq K\), and the definition of \(e\) imply
\[
E_I^{\mathrm{act}}-E_I^{\mathrm{virt}}
=\frac1{|I|}\sum_{k\in I}E_k^{\mathrm{virt}}
 \{\exp(eQ_k)-1\}
>\frac{20-\delta}{K}\{\exp(e\eta)-1\}
=2\delta.
\tag{4}
\]
If \(a_j(x,q)>-\delta\), every intersection containing \(j\) has
\(E_I>20-\delta\); hence (4) gives
\(a_j(x+eq,q)\geq a_j(x,q)+2\delta\).
If instead \(a_j(x,q)\leq-\delta\), then
\(f_\delta^-(a_j(x,q))=1\).  Checking these two cases in the displayed
definitions of \(f_\delta^\pm\) proves the pointwise inequality
\[
f_\delta^+\!\left(a_j(x+eq,q)\right)
\leq f_\delta^-\!\left(a_j(x,q)\right)
\quad\text{on }\mathcal E_{\eta,\delta}^c.
\tag{5}
\]
Multiplication by the nonnegative loss weights and summation preserve (5).

Apply (5) under drift \(h^m+e\mathbf 1\), where the virtual terminal state has
the original law at \(h^m\), and then use (2) to return the transformed policy
to drift \(h^m\).  Since the losses are bounded by one, (2), (3), and (5) give,
simultaneously for all \(m\),
\[
\mathbb E_m^{\pi_n^e}[\ell_{m,\delta}^+]
\leq
\mathbb E_m^{\pi_n}[\ell_{m,\delta}^-]
+\frac e2
+2K\exp\!\left[
-\frac{(\log(20-\delta)-H\eta)_+^2}{2\eta}
\right],
\tag{6}
\]
with the right side truncated at one.  The same calculation holds for
\(u^e\) and \(u\).  Weighting (6) by any \(\lambda\in\Delta_M\), then taking
the infimum over the original comparator policy, gives exactly
\[
B_{n,\delta}^+(\lambda)-B_{n,\delta}^-(\lambda)
\leq\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\eta),
\qquad
B_\delta^+(\lambda)-B_\delta^-(\lambda)
\leq\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\eta).
\]
Taking a point-mass prior proves the identical oracle inequalities.

No positive clock was assumed.  In the unsampled-subgroup stress test,
\(Q_j=0\) forces \(X_j=0\) and \(E_j=1<20-\delta\), so that coordinate cannot
witness a near-critical intersection.  In the hit-and-freeze stress test,
a frozen value \(E_j=20\) either has \(Q_j\leq\eta\), in which case it is
already charged to (3), or has \(Q_j>\eta\), in which case (4) moves it
strictly above the boundary.  Thus both \(K=2\) kill tests pass without
forced exploration.

Finally put \(\eta=\sqrt\delta\).  Since \(20-\delta\geq19\),
\[
\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{shift}}(\delta,\sqrt\delta)}2
\leq \frac{K\sqrt\delta}{19},
\]
where \(\log(1+z)\leq z\) was used.  Moreover
\(\log(20-\delta)-H\sqrt\delta\to\log20>0\), so the exponential term in
\(\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\sqrt\delta)\) tends to zero.  This proves the asserted
limit.

We prove separately the exact embedding, regular-payoff approximation, the
boundary squeeze, and policy attainment.

\emph{Exact embedding.}
Fix \(n\) and \(\pi_n\in\Pi_n\).  On
\(((i-1)/n,i/n]\), let the continuous control be the vertex
\[
u_j(t)=\mathbf 1\{A_i=j\}.
\]
It is observed-filtration predictable by Assumption
\(\mathrm{ass:finite\text{-}predictability}\), hence admissible under
Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:continuous\text{-}observed\text{-}control}\).
Conditionally on the history and \(A_i=j\), its score increment is
\[
\Delta X_j=\frac{h_j^m}{n}
+W_j(i/n)-W_j((i-1)/n)
\sim\mathcal N(h_j^m/n,1/n),
\]
and its clock increment is \(1/n\); all other coordinates have zero
increments.  By Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass:gaussian\text{-}known\text{-}variance}\)
and \(\mathrm{ass:local\text{-}scenario\text{-}scaling}\),
\(Y_i/\sqrt n\) has exactly the same conditional law.  Induction over \(i\)
therefore gives equality of the complete observed laws, not merely weak
convergence.  Thus every finite policy is a vertex-control diffusion policy
and has exactly the same risk vector.

\emph{Approximation for continuous terminal payoffs.}
Let \(g_m:\mathbb R^K\times[0,1]^K\to[0,1]\) be bounded and continuous, for
\(m=1,\ldots,M\).  We claim that the infimal prior-weighted risk over the
embedded \(n\)-grid controls converges to the infimum over \(\mathcal U\).
Here is the construction in the present Gaussian experiment.

On the canonical observed space, every progressively measurable
\(\Delta(\mathcal J)\)-valued control is approximable in
\(dt\,d\mathbb P_0\)-measure by simple predictable controls: first replace it
by conditional averages on a deterministic time partition, and then
approximate each past-measurable simplex-valued random variable by a finite
simple function.  Boundedness upgrades convergence in measure to
\[
\mathbb E_0\int_0^1\sum_j|u_j^{(r)}(t)-u_j(t)|\,dt\longrightarrow0.
\tag{7}
\]
For a fixed simple control, subdivide each of its time cells into \(n\)-grid
cells and, conditionally on the information at the left endpoint, choose
vertex \(j\) with its declared simplex probability.  Conditional variances
of the centered allocation counts sum to at most \(1/n\), so the cumulative
clock error tends to zero in probability.  Conditional on those counts, the
score increment in coordinate \(j\) is exactly Gaussian with mean
\(h_j^m\Delta Q_j\) and variance \(\Delta Q_j\).  Therefore its conditional
characteristic function is
\[
\exp\!\left\{\mathrm i z_jh_j^m\Delta Q_j
-\frac12z_j^2\Delta Q_j\right\},
\]
which converges to the characteristic function of the corresponding relaxed
Gaussian transition.  Induction over the finitely many simple-control cells
proves joint convergence of the terminal score and clock.  Past-measurable
simple functions may be chosen continuous outside sets of arbitrarily small
probability under all of the finitely many scenario laws; changing them on
those sets changes any bounded risk by at most that probability.  A diagonal
choice in \(r\) and \(n\) therefore gives grid policies
\(\pi_n[u]\) such that
\[
(X_n,Q_n)\ \Longrightarrow\ (X^u(1),Q^u(1))
\quad\text{under every }m.
\tag{8}
\]
This construction uses vertex choices even when some simplex coordinates
are zero, so it imposes no exploration lower bound.

One can also see directly that the change from the reference law to every
scenario is harmless in (8).  Under drift zero, the likelihood ratio is
\[
Z_m(X,Q)=
\exp\!\left\{\sum_jh_j^mX_j-\frac12
\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j\right\}.
\tag{9}
\]
The assignment factors cancel because the policy is scenario independent.
Furthermore,
\[
\mathbb E_0[Z_m(X,Q)^2]
\leq\exp(H^2),
\tag{10}
\]
because \(\sum_jQ_j=1\) and \(|h_j^m|\leq H\).  Thus the likelihood ratios
are uniformly integrable, and reference-law convergence transfers to all
\(M\) scenario laws.  Equations (7)--(10), bounded continuity of \(g_m\),
and an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal choice of \(u\) show
\[
\inf_{\pi_n\in\Pi_n}\sum_m\lambda_m\mathbb E_m^{\pi_n}g_m
\longrightarrow
\inf_{u\in\mathcal U}\sum_m\lambda_m\mathbb E_m^ug_m
\tag{11}
\]
for each \(\lambda\).  The reverse inequality needed in (11) holds at every
\(n\) because of the exact embedding.  This proves the regular-payoff
approximation from the primitive Gaussian transitions rather than assuming
a limit law.

For fixed \(\delta>0\), the functions
\(\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm\) from Definition
\(\mathrm{def:terminal\text{-}envelopes}\) are bounded and continuous:
exponentiation, finite averages, and finite minima are continuous, as are
\(f_\delta^\pm\).  Applying (11) yields
\[
B_{n,\delta}^\pm(\lambda)\longrightarrow
B_\delta^\pm(\lambda).
\tag{12}
\]
Every one of the four value functions in (12) is \(1\)-Lipschitz in
\(\lambda\) for the \(\ell_1\) norm, because each scenario risk lies in
\([0,1]\).  A finite \(\ell_1\)-net of the compact simplex \(\Delta_M\)
therefore upgrades (12) to convergence uniform in \(\lambda\).

\emph{Removal of the continuous envelopes.}
The scalar bracketing proved in
\(\mathrm{lem:quantitative\text{-}terminal\text{-}comparison}\) gives
\[
B_{n,\delta}^-(\lambda)\leq B_n(\lambda)\leq
B_{n,\delta}^+(\lambda),
\qquad
B_\delta^-(\lambda)\leq B(\lambda)\leq B_\delta^+(\lambda).
\]
Combining these inequalities with (12) gives
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
\leq\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\sqrt\delta).
\]
Letting \(\delta\downarrow0\) and using the last conclusion of
\(\mathrm{lem:quantitative\text{-}terminal\text{-}comparison}\) proves
\[
\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{13}
\]
For the point-mass prior \(e_m\), the definitions give
\(B_n(e_m)=c_{n,m}\) and \(B(e_m)=c_m\).  Hence (13) proves
\[
\max_{1\leq m\leq M}|c_{n,m}-c_m|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{14}
\]

For completeness, we derive the finite-scenario minimax identity needed to
pass from (13)--(14) to regret values.  Let \(C_n\) be the closure in
\([0,1]^M\) of the achievable regret vectors.  Independent randomization at
time zero makes it convex, and closure makes it compact without changing the
infimum of any continuous criterion.  Since
\(\max_m r_m=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\lambda^\top r\), finite-dimensional
convex separation gives
\[
\inf_{r\in C_n}\max_mr_m
=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\inf_{r\in C_n}\lambda^\top r.
\tag{15}
\]
To verify the direction in (15), put \(v=\inf_{r\in C_n}\max_mr_m\).
The upward-closed convex set \(C_n+\mathbb R_+^M\) has \(v\mathbf1\) on its
boundary.  Projecting \((v-k^{-1})\mathbf1\) onto this set and taking a
convergent subsequence of the normalized projection normals produces
\(\lambda\geq0\), \(\sum_m\lambda_m=1\), with
\(\lambda^\top r\geq v\) for every \(r\in C_n\).  The opposite inequality
follows from \(\lambda^\top r\leq\max_mr_m\).  This proves (15)
elementarily.  Translating back from regret to loss yields
\[
V_n=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
\left\{B_n(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{n,m}\right\},
\]
and the identical argument gives the corresponding formula for \(V\).
Consequently,
\[
|V_n-V|
\leq\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
+\max_m|c_{n,m}-c_m|\longrightarrow0
\]
by (13)--(14).

\emph{Predictable policy attainment.}
Fix \(\epsilon>0\).  Choose a finite integer \(N\) so large that
\(|V_N-V|+\max_m|c_{N,m}-c_m|<\epsilon/3\), and choose
\(\pi_N\in\Pi_N\) with
\[
\max_m\{L_N(\pi_N,m)-c_{N,m}\}\leq V_N+\epsilon/3.
\]
Embed \(\pi_N\) as the \(N\)-block vertex control \(u^\epsilon\) constructed
above.  Exact equality of risk vectors and the preceding bounds show
\[
\max_m r_m(u^\epsilon)\leq V+\epsilon.
\tag{16}
\]
This is an \(\epsilon\)-optimal diffusion control.

It remains to approximate this particular control without invoking
continuity of an arbitrary stopped diffusion payoff.  Conditional on an
exogenous random seed and on any of the finitely many action sequences of
\(\pi_N\), the \(N\) observed Gaussian outcomes have a Lebesgue density.
Every terminal threshold equality is contained in a finite union of zero
sets of functions
\[
\sum_{j\in I}\exp(X_j-Q_j/2)-20|I|.
\]
Such a function is nonconstant whenever one of its coordinates was sampled;
if none was sampled its value is \(|I|-20|I|\neq0\).  Its zero set therefore
has Lebesgue measure zero.  Hence
\[
\Pr_m^{u^\epsilon}\{a_j(X(1),Q(1))=0
\text{ for some }j\}=0
\quad\text{for every }m.
\tag{17}
\]
At horizon \(n\), divide the observations into \(N\) consecutive blocks
whose lengths differ from \(n/N\) by at most one, keep the arm selected by
\(\pi_N\) throughout a block, and feed the next decision the block aggregate.
This is a predictable finite policy.  Each aggregate is exactly Gaussian
with clock length converging to \(1/N\); induction over the fixed number
\(N\) of blocks gives convergence of its terminal state to that of
\(u^\epsilon\).  Arbitrary measurable recruitment kernels of \(\pi_N\) may
first be changed on sets of arbitrarily small probability under the finite
family of Gaussian history laws so that this induction is valid at their
continuity points.  Equation (17) then permits the ordinary bounded
continuous-mapping argument for the original strict miss indicators.
Thus the resulting predictable policies \(\pi_n^\epsilon\) satisfy
\[
L_n(\pi_n^\epsilon,m)\longrightarrow L(u^\epsilon,m)
\quad\text{for every }m.
\]
Together with (16), this proves the asserted coordinatewise risk transfer.
The construction permits zero block allocations to every unused subgroup,
so arbitrary predictable policies and zero-allocation faces are retained.
Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:null\text{-}boundary\text{-}closure}\) ensures that
all intersection-null boundary projections invoked by the declared design
remain within the fixed finite scenario set; the auxiliary common drift used
in the comparison proof is only a change-of-measure device and does not
enlarge that set.

We give one argument that applies to the finite and diffusion experiments.
Write \(\mathcal A\) for the relevant policy class and
\[
r(a)=(L(a,1)-c_1,\ldots,L(a,M)-c_M)\in[0,1]^M,
\]
using \(n\)-subscripts in the finite experiment.  Let
\[
C:=\overline{\{r(a):a\in\mathcal A\}}\subset[0,1]^M.
\]
Time-zero randomization, which is allowed by both Definitions
\(\mathrm{def:finite\text{-}policy\text{-}class}\) and
\(\mathrm{def:continuous\text{-}control\text{-}class}\), makes \(C\) convex;
it is compact by construction.

Put \(v=\min_{r\in C}\max_mr_m\).  The set
\(D=C+\mathbb R_+^M\) is closed and convex, and \(v\mathbf1\) is a boundary
point of \(D\).  Indeed, compactness attains the minimum, so some
\(r^\star\in C\) satisfies \(r^\star\leq v\mathbf1\), whereas
\((v-a)\mathbf1\notin D\) for every \(a>0\).  Project
\((v-k^{-1})\mathbf1\) onto \(D\).  The projection inequality, followed by
normalization and passage to a subsequence, supplies a nonzero supporting
normal \(\lambda^\star\).  Because \(D\) is upward closed, every coordinate
of this normal is nonnegative; normalize it so that
\(\sum_m\lambda_m^\star=1\).  The support inequality is
\[
\lambda^{\star\top}r\geq
\lambda^{\star\top}(v\mathbf1)=v
\quad\text{for every }r\in C.
\tag{18}
\]
Conversely, for every \(\lambda\in\Delta_M\),
\(\lambda^\top r\leq\max_mr_m\), whence
\[
\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\min_{r\in C}\lambda^\top r=v.
\tag{19}
\]
No continuity of the terminal loss was used in this finite-dimensional
separation.

Closure does not alter an infimum of a linear functional.  In the finite
experiment,
\[
\inf_{r\in C}\lambda^\top r
=\inf_{\pi_n\in\Pi_n}\sum_m\lambda_m
\{L_n(\pi_n,m)-c_{n,m}\}
=B_n(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{n,m}.
\]
The same calculation with \(u\in\mathcal U\) gives
\(B(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_m\).  Substitution in (19) proves both
displayed minimax identities.  The dual objective is \(1\)-Lipschitz:
\[
\left|\inf_{r\in C}\lambda^\top r-
\inf_{r\in C}\lambda'^\top r\right|
\leq\sup_{r\in[0,1]^M}|(\lambda-\lambda')^\top r|
\leq\|\lambda-\lambda'\|_1.
\]
It is therefore continuous on compact \(\Delta_M\), so a least-favorable
prior is attained in both experiments.

We next identify the sufficient posterior state and the saddle response.
Fix a prior \(\lambda\).  Under the zero-drift reference law and any
scenario-independent observed control, conditional Gaussian integration
gives the likelihood ratio
\[
Z_m(X(t),Q(t))
=\exp\!\left\{\sum_jh_j^mX_j(t)
-\frac12\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j(t)\right\}.
\tag{20}
\]
The denominator \(\sum_r\lambda_rZ_r\) is strictly positive because every
\(Z_r>0\) and at least one \(\lambda_r>0\).  Bayes' formula and (20) give
\[
\Pr\{m\mid\mathcal F_t\}
=\frac{\lambda_mZ_m(X(t),Q(t))}
{\sum_r\lambda_rZ_r(X(t),Q(t))}
=b_m^\lambda(X(t),Q(t)).
\tag{21}
\]
Moreover,
\[
\sum_m\lambda_mL(u,m)
=\mathbb E_0^u\!\left[
\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m(X(1),Q(1))\ell_m(X(1),Q(1))
\right].
\tag{22}
\]
Thus the Bayes control problem is a terminal-cost Markov problem in
\((t,X,Q,b^\lambda)\), with \(b^\lambda\) itself the deterministic function
in (21).

For clarity, Markovization can be obtained directly in this Gaussian model.
For a relaxed observed control, disintegrate its action at time \(t\)
conditionally on \((X(t),Q(t),b^\lambda(t))\), and use that conditional
simplex vector as the randomized Markov action.  For simple controls,
iterated conditional Gaussian kernels show by induction that this operation
preserves the terminal reference-law distribution.  Approximation by simple
predictable controls, using the bounded-energy estimate (10) from the proof
of \(\mathrm{thm:boundary\text{-}stable\text{-}frontier}\), extends the
identity to all admissible relaxed controls.  Equations (20)--(22) then show
that it preserves every scenario risk, not only their Bayes average.
Consequently every Bayes response may be chosen Markov in the state displayed
in the theorem.

Finally choose the attained least-favorable prior \(\lambda^\star\).
The compact weak relaxed-control formulation attains the nonnegative,
lower-semicontinuous Bayes terminal cost: each
\(\mathbf1\{a_j<0\}\) is lower semicontinuous because \(a_j\) is continuous,
and (22) has the positive continuous likelihood weights.  Equivalently, one
may take a minimizing sequence, extract a weak relaxed-control limit, and
apply the defining open-set inequality term by term.  Let \(F\) be the set
of risk vectors of its Bayes best responses.  From (18), every member of
\(F\) has \(\lambda^{\star\top}r=V\).  A minimax vector
\(r^\star\in C\) satisfies \(r^\star\leq V\mathbf1\), and
\[
V\leq\lambda^{\star\top}r^\star\leq V,
\]
so \(r^\star\) lies in the exposed Bayes face.  Approximating within that
face by attained Markov Bayes responses and applying the finite-dimensional
Carathéodory reduction yields a mixture of at most \(M+1\) such responses
whose risk vector is at most \((V+\epsilon)\mathbf1\).  The mixture seed is
drawn at time zero and included in the exogenous randomization, so the
mixture remains admissible and each component is Markov in
\((t,X,Q,b^{\lambda^\star})\).

For this mixture \(u^\epsilon\), for every nature prior \(\lambda\),
\[
\sum_m\lambda_mr_m(u^\epsilon)\leq V+\epsilon,
\]
while for every control \(u\), (18) gives
\[
\sum_m\lambda_m^\star r_m(u)\geq V.
\]
These are the two saddle inequalities, and taking point-mass \(\lambda\)
in the first one gives \(r_m(u^\epsilon)\leq V+\epsilon\) for every
scenario.  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:null\text{-}boundary\text{-}closure}\)
keeps all of these best responses and priors on the declared finite scenario
game; it is not used to add an unlisted alternative.

open_obligations.what_is_open: The asserted eight-part interval error ledger is not determined by the frozen certificate handle.
open_obligations.obstruction: The handle does not specify the boundary extension, the interval interpolation formulas, the Gaussian cell enclosures, or a proved consistency estimate with the displayed constants. Monotonicity and finiteness alone cannot imply the requested numerical width.
open_obligations.attempted: I verified termination of every explicitly finite loop, the advertised transition-count bound, and the regularization, score-tail, prior-net, and accumulated-rounding budgets. The remaining interpolation, quadrature, oracle-offset, and policy-evaluation bounds require missing algorithmic formulas and stability estimates.
open_obligations.partial_result:
The parts forced by the displayed formulas can be certified.  Put
\(a=2^{-r_\delta}=\eta_{\mathrm{cert}}\) and
\(\delta_{\mathrm{cert}}=a^2\).  The definition of \(r_\delta\) implies
\[
a\leq\frac{19\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}}{32K},\qquad
Ha\leq\frac{\log19}{2},\qquad
a\leq\frac{(\log19)^2}
{8\log(64K/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}})}.
\]
Since \(20-a^2\geq19\) and \(\log(1+x)\leq x\),
\[
\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{shift}}(a^2,a)}2
\leq\frac{Ka}{19}\leq\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}}{32},
\]
and
\[
2K\exp\!\left\{
-\frac{(\log(20-a^2)-Ha)^2}{2a}\right\}
\leq\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}}{32}.
\]
Thus the proved terminal comparison spends at most
\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}/16\), in particular at most the advertised
\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}/8\).

The score-stack representation also gives
\[
\sup_{m,u}\Pr_m^u\!\left\{
\max_j\sup_{t\leq1}|X_j(t)|>R_{\mathrm{cert}}\right\}
\leq4K\exp\!\left\{
-\frac{(R_{\mathrm{cert}}-H)^2}{2}\right\}
=\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}}{32}.
\]
The dual regret functional is \(1\)-Lipschitz in the prior's \(\ell_1\)
distance, so the displayed prior net costs at most
\(r_{\lambda,\mathrm{cert}}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}/32\).
Finally all mesh cardinalities are finite positive integers.  There are at
most
\[
MKN_{\mathrm{prior}}N_{\mathrm{state}}N_{\mathrm{quad}}
\]
listed interval-transition evaluations, and
\[
MKN_{\mathrm{prior}}N_{\mathrm{state}}N_{\mathrm{quad}}
\,2^{-p_{\mathrm{cert}}}
\leq\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}}{512}
\]
for one unit of outward-rounding error per evaluation.  Hence these loops
terminate and the final finite linear program terminates.  What is not
derivable is that the unspecified interpolation and Gaussian-cell
operations enclose the true Bellman semigroup with the remaining advertised
budgets; that missing estimate is exactly the unresolved part of
\(\mathrm{thm:certified\text{-}dynamic\text{-}program}\).

open_obligations.what_is_open: Comparison and uniqueness at every viable off-origin state remain unproved.
open_obligations.obstruction: The common-drift translation changes only future information from an off-origin state. A coordinate frozen after that state receives no strict terminal displacement, so the origin argument does not order the two generalized terminal traces there.
open_obligations.attempted: I propagated the shift coupling on the remaining time interval and checked zero-allocation faces. This reproduces the initial-state squeeze only when every near-critical intersection contains a coordinate receiving enough future clock; that property fails on general viable faces and cannot be imposed without changing the control class.
open_obligations.partial_result:
Starting from a viable state \((t_0,x,q)\), the same common-drift coupling
changes only future scores:
\[
X_j(s)\longmapsto X_j(s)+e\{Q_j(s)-q_j\},
\qquad t_0\leq s\leq1,
\]
and its relative-entropy cost is
\[
\frac{e^2}{2}\sum_j\{Q_j(1)-q_j\}
=\frac{e^2}{2}(1-t_0).
\]
Thus the initial-state comparison proof extends statewise whenever every
intersection within \(\delta\) of threshold contains a coordinate whose
remaining allocation is at least a declared positive amount.  At the
origin this follows without forced exploration because an unsampled
coordinate has \(X_j=Q_j=0\) and elementary e-value one.  At a general
off-origin state, however, a near-critical intersection can be supported
entirely on coordinates receiving zero future clock.  Its terminal value is
then unchanged by every such translation.  The quantitative initial-state
squeeze is therefore proved, but it supplies neither an ordering of the two
generalized terminal traces nor comparison on all of \(\mathcal D\).

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix a policy \(\pi_n\in\Pi_n\), a mean vector \(\mu\), and a subgroup \(j\in\mathcal J\).  Write
\[
D_{j,i}:=\mathbf 1\{A_i=j\},\qquad
Z_{j,s}:=\sum_{i=1}^s D_{j,i}(Y_i-\mu_j)
=S_{j,s}-\mu_jN_{j,s},\qquad
V_{j,s}:=N_{j,s}.
\]
For \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), define
\[
\mathcal E_{j,s}(\lambda)
:=\exp\!\left\{\lambda Z_{j,s}-\frac{\lambda^2}{2}V_{j,s}\right\},
\qquad \mathcal E_{j,0}(\lambda)=1.
\]
We first verify the supermartingale premise rather than assuming it.  By predictability in Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}finite\mbox{-}predictability}\), the conditional probabilities
\(p_{i,a}:=\mathbb P(A_i=a\mid\mathcal F_{i-1})\) are \(\mathcal F_{i-1}\)-measurable.  Conditioning first on \(A_i\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_\mu\!\left[
\left.\frac{\mathcal E_{j,i}(\lambda)}{\mathcal E_{j,i-1}(\lambda)}
\right|\mathcal F_{i-1}\right]
&=\sum_{a\in\mathcal J}p_{i,a}\,
\mathbb E_\mu\!\left[
\left.\exp\!\left\{D_{j,i}\left(\lambda(Y_i-\mu_j)-\frac{\lambda^2}{2}\right)\right\}
\right|\mathcal F_{i-1},A_i=a\right]\\
&=\sum_{a\neq j}p_{i,a}
+p_{i,j}\exp\!\left\{-\frac{\lambda^2}{2}\right\}
\mathbb E\!\left[e^{\lambda G}\right],
\qquad G\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\\
&=\sum_{a\neq j}p_{i,a}+p_{i,j}=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
The second equality uses Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}gaussian\mbox{-}known\mbox{-}variance}\), and the third uses the Gaussian moment-generating identity
\(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda G}]=e^{\lambda^2/2}\).  Hence \((\mathcal E_{j,s}(\lambda))_{s=0}^n\) is a nonnegative martingale, and therefore a nonnegative supermartingale, for every \(\lambda\).

Apply Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}howard\mbox{-}linear\mbox{-}boundary}\) with \(\lambda=n^{-1/2}\) and \(\beta=\gamma_j\).  These substitutions are legal because \(n\geq1\), while positivity of the normalized weights gives \(0<\gamma_j=\alpha w_j<1\).  Restricting its crossing event to the finite horizon gives
\[
\mathbb P_\mu\!\left\{\exists,0\leq s\leq n:
Z_{j,s}\geq \sqrt n\log(1/\gamma_j)+\frac{N_{j,s}}{2\sqrt n}\right\}
\leq\gamma_j.
\tag{1}
\]
At any \(s\) for which \(N_{j,s}>0\), Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}confidence\mbox{-}inversion}\) and elementary multiplication by the positive quantity \(N_{j,s}\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_j<B_{j,s}
&\iff
\mu_j<\frac{S_{j,s}}{N_{j,s}}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt n}
-\frac{\sqrt n}{N_{j,s}}\log(1/\gamma_j)\\
&\iff
S_{j,s}-\mu_jN_{j,s}>
\frac{N_{j,s}}{2\sqrt n}+\sqrt n\log(1/\gamma_j)\\
&\iff
Z_{j,s}>
\sqrt n\log(1/\gamma_j)+\frac{N_{j,s}}{2\sqrt n}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]
If \(N_{j,s}=0\), the same definition sets \(B_{j,s}=-\infty\), so \(\{\mu_j<B_{j,s}\}\) is empty.  Thus (2), followed by the weak-threshold crossing bound (1), yields
\[
\mathbb P_\mu\!\left\{\exists,0\leq s\leq n:\mu_j<B_{j,s}\right\}\leq\gamma_j.
\tag{3}
\]
Finally, \(\mathcal J\) is finite, so the union bound, the calibration \(\gamma_j=\alpha w_j\), and \(\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}w_j=1\) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P_\mu\!\left\{\exists j\in\mathcal J,\ 0\leq s\leq n:
\mu_j<B_{j,s}\right\}
&\leq\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}\gamma_j\\
&=\alpha\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}w_j
=\alpha.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking complements proves
\[
\mathbb P_\mu\!\left\{\mu_j\geq B_{j,s}
\text{ for all }j\in\mathcal J\text{ and }0\leq s\leq n\right\}
\geq1-\alpha.
\]
Because the policy was arbitrary, the conclusion holds for every predictable policy, including policies that never sample some subgroup.

added_lemmas.statement:
Linear uniform boundary.  Let \((Z_s,V_s)_{s\geq 0}\) be adapted processes with \(Z_0=V_0=0\) and \(V_s\geq 0\).  Suppose that, for every \(\lambda>0\), the process
\[
\exp\!\left\{\lambda Z_s-\frac{\lambda^2}{2}V_s\right\},\qquad s\geq 0,
\]
is a nonnegative supermartingale with initial value at most one.  Then, for every \(\lambda>0\) and \(\beta\in(0,1)\),
\[
\mathbb P\!\left\{\exists s\geq 0:
Z_s\geq \frac{\log(1/\beta)}{\lambda}+\frac{\lambda}{2}V_s\right\}\leq\beta.
\]

source.verbatim_statement: For any \(\lambda\in[0,\lambda_{\max})\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), \(u(v)\coloneqq\frac{\log(l_0/\alpha)}{\lambda}+\frac{\psi(\lambda)}{\lambda}\cdot v\) is a sub-\(\psi\) uniform boundary with crossing probability \(\alpha\).

attestation.note: Transcribed from Howard et al. (2021), Lemma 1, equations (6)--(7).

proposed.statement: Supporting corollary (Howard et al. and Ville inversion): for every predictable policy and every mean vector \(\mu=(\mu_j)_{j\in\mathcal J}\), \(\mathbb P_\mu\{\mu_j\geq B_{j,s}\text{ for all }j\in\mathcal J\text{ and }0\leq s\leq n\}\geq1-\alpha\). If \(N_{j,s}=0\), then \(B_{j,s}=-\infty\).
proposed.justification: This cited Ville-inversion corollary supplies simultaneous reporting alongside the optimized design; it is not a novelty-bearing result.
proposed.gap: Howard et al. provide time-uniform supermartingale inversion; subgroupwise allocation of error and a union bound give this direct supporting corollary, including the zero-information endpoint.
proposed.consumer: Trial reports obtain simultaneous one-sided effect sequences even when the optimal policy stops sampling a subgroup.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Declare the cited linear-boundary result used by the proof as a direct dependency.

proofs.proof_tex:
Let \(m_0,m_1,m_2\) denote the three scenario labels for which \(h^{m_0}=(0,0)\), \(h^{m_1}=(1,0)\), and \(h^{m_2}=(0,1)\), respectively.  Because \(n=1\), there is no observed response before the only recruitment decision.  Definition~\texttt{def:finite-policy-class} and Assumption~\texttt{ass:finite-predictability} therefore imply that every admissible policy is summarized, for purposes of its law, by the scenario-independent number
\[
 p:=\Pr_{\pi_1}(A_1=1)\in[0,1],
 \qquad
 \Pr_{\pi_1}(A_1=2)=1-p.
\]
Conversely, every \(p\in[0,1]\) is feasible by randomizing \(A_1\) with these probabilities before observing \(Y_1\).  Hence optimization over \(\Pi_1\) is exactly optimization over \(p\in[0,1]\).

Suppose first that \(A_1=1\).  The definitions of the normalized score and allocation clock give
\[
 (X_{1,1},Q_{1,1})=(Y_1,1),
 \qquad
 (X_{2,1},Q_{2,1})=(0,0).
\]
Thus Definition~\texttt{def:fixed-closed-e-test} gives
\[
 E_{1,1}=e:=\exp(Y_1-1/2),
 \qquad E_{2,1}=1.
\]
For the sampled subgroup, the only intersections containing subgroup \(1\) are \(\{1\}\) and \(\{1,2\}\).  Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 1\in\mathcal R_1
 &\iff \min\left\{e-20,\frac{e+1}{2}-20\right\}\geq0 \\
 &\iff e\geq20\ \text{ and }\ e\geq39 \\
 &\iff Y_1\geq \tau,
 \qquad \tau:=\log 39+\frac12.
\end{aligned}
\]
The unsampled subgroup cannot be rejected, since its singleton-intersection margin is \(E_{2,1}-20=1-20<0\).  Exchanging subgroup labels proves the corresponding facts when \(A_1=2\).

Under either one-positive scenario, Assumption~\texttt{ass:local-scenario-scaling} with \(n=1\) makes the mean in the active subgroup equal to \(1\), and Assumption~\texttt{ass:gaussian-known-variance} makes its response \(\mathcal N(1,1)\).  Define
\[
 \beta:=\Pr\{\mathcal N(1,1)\geq\tau\}
 =\overline\Phi(\tau-1)
 =\overline\Phi(\log 39-1/2).
\]
By the displayed positive Gaussian-density integral defining \(\overline\Phi\), \(0<\beta<1\).  The active subgroup is therefore discovered with probability \(\beta\) when it is sampled and with probability \(0\) when it is not sampled.

For brevity, write \(L_1(p,m)\) for \(L_1(\pi_1,m)\) when \(\pi_1\) has allocation probability \(p\), and similarly write \(r_{1,m}(p)\) for its regret.  The loss definition assigns weight \(1/2\) to the single positive subgroup.  Conditioning on \(A_1\) now yields, equation by equation,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 L_1(p,m_1)
 &=\frac12\bigl[p(1-\beta)+(1-p)\bigr]
 =\frac12(1-p\beta),\\
 L_1(p,m_2)
 &=\frac12\bigl[p+(1-p)(1-\beta)\bigr]
 =\frac12\bigl(1-(1-p)\beta\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(m_0\), every factor \(\mathbf 1\{h_j^{m_0}>0\}\) in \(\ell_{m_0}\) is zero, so
\[
 L_1(p,m_0)=0.
\]
Since \(\beta>0\), the first one-positive risk is minimized at \(p=1\), the second at \(p=0\), and the null risk is already zero.  Hence the oracle quantities in Definition~\texttt{def:minimax-regret} are
\[
 c_{1,m_0}=0,
 \qquad
 c_{1,m_1}=c_{1,m_2}=\frac12(1-\beta).
\]
Subtracting these oracle risks gives
\[
 r_{1,m_0}(p)=0,
 \qquad
 r_{1,m_1}(p)=\frac{\beta}{2}(1-p),
 \qquad
 r_{1,m_2}(p)=\frac{\beta}{2}p.
\]
Using again Definition~\texttt{def:minimax-regret} and the exact reduction of \(\Pi_1\) to \([0,1]\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 V_1
 &=\inf_{0\leq p\leq1}\frac{\beta}{2}\max\{p,1-p\}\\
 &=\frac{\beta}{2}\inf_{0\leq p\leq1}
 \left(\frac12+\left|p-\frac12\right|\right)\\
 &=\frac{\beta}{4}
 =\frac14\overline\Phi(\log 39-1/2),
\end{aligned}
\]
with equality attained by the symmetric policy \(p=1/2\), as claimed.
